introduction.heading: Chemical Reactions: The Magic of Transformation
introduction.details_en: Consider the situations of daily life: milk left at room temperature during summers, iron pans getting rusted, grapes fermenting, or food getting digested in our body. In all these situations, the nature and identity of the initial substance have somewhat changed. Whenever a chemical change occurs, we say a chemical reaction has taken place. This chapter dives deep into understanding these reactions, how to represent them using chemical equations, and the different types of chemical reactions.

key_definitions.explanation_en: A process in which one or more substances (reactants) are converted into one or more different substances (products) with new physical and chemical properties.
The substances which take part in a chemical reaction. They are written on the left-hand side (LHS) of a chemical equation.
The new substances produced as a result of a chemical reaction. They are written on the right-hand side (RHS) of a chemical equation.
The symbolic representation of a chemical reaction using symbols and chemical formulae of the reactants and products.
An unbalanced chemical equation that only shows the reactants and products without satisfying the Law of Conservation of Mass (the number of atoms of each element is not equal on both sides).
A chemical equation in which the number of atoms of each element is equal on both the reactant side and the product side.
A reaction in which two or more reactants combine to form a single product. (e.g., A + B → AB)
A reaction in which a single reactant breaks down to form two or more simpler products. It requires energy in the form of heat, light, or electricity. (e.g., AB → A + B)
A reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. (e.g., A + BC → AC + B)
A reaction in which there is an exchange of ions between two reactants to form new compounds. (e.g., AB + CD → AD + CB)
Any reaction that produces an insoluble solid (precipitate) which separates from the solution.
The process of addition of oxygen to a substance or the removal of hydrogen from a substance.
The process of addition of hydrogen to a substance or the removal of oxygen from a substance.
A reaction in which one reactant gets oxidized while the other gets reduced simultaneously.
The slow eating away of metals by the action of air, moisture, or chemicals on their surface (e.g., rusting of iron).
The slow oxidation of oils and fats present in food materials resulting in a bad smell and taste.

practical_examples.title: Burning of Magnesium Ribbon
practical_examples.problem: Describe the reaction when a magnesium ribbon is burnt in air. Why should it be cleaned before burning?
practical_examples.solution:
Reaction: Magnesium ribbon burns with a dazzling white flame and changes into a white powder (magnesium oxide). 
Equation: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s)
Reason for cleaning: It is cleaned with sandpaper to remove the protective layer of basic magnesium carbonate so it can readily react with oxygen.

practical_examples.title: Formation of Slaked Lime (Combination Reaction)
practical_examples.problem: What happens when water is added to quicklime (Calcium Oxide)?
practical_examples.solution:
Quicklime reacts vigorously with water to form slaked lime (Calcium Hydroxide) releasing a large amount of heat. 
Equation: CaO(s) + H2O(l) → Ca(OH)2(aq) + Heat
This is an exothermic combination reaction.

practical_examples.title: Thermal Decomposition of Ferrous Sulphate
practical_examples.problem: Explain the changes observed when ferrous sulphate crystals are heated in a dry boiling tube.
practical_examples.solution:
The green colour of ferrous sulphate crystals (FeSO4·7H2O) changes, and it breaks down into solid ferric oxide, sulphur dioxide, and sulphur trioxide gases. You can smell the characteristic odour of burning sulphur.
Equation: 2FeSO4(s) + Heat → Fe2O3(s) + SO2(g) + SO3(g)

practical_examples.title: Electrolysis of Water (Decomposition by Electricity)
practical_examples.problem: What are the products formed during the electrolysis of water? What is the ratio of their volumes?
practical_examples.solution:
Water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen gases when electricity is passed through it.
Equation: 2H2O(l) + Electricity → 2H2(g) + O2(g)
Hydrogen is collected at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. The volume ratio of H2 to O2 is 2:1.

practical_examples.title: Photochemical Decomposition of Silver Chloride
practical_examples.problem: Why is silver chloride stored in dark-coloured bottles?
practical_examples.solution:
Silver chloride turns grey in sunlight because it decomposes into silver and chlorine gas due to light. Storing it in dark bottles prevents light from entering and stops this decomposition.
Equation: 2AgCl(s) + Sunlight → 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g)

practical_examples.title: Displacement of Copper by Iron
practical_examples.problem: What happens when iron nails are placed in a copper sulphate solution?
practical_examples.solution:
Iron is more reactive than copper. It displaces copper from copper sulphate solution. The blue colour of copper sulphate fades to light green (due to iron sulphate), and a brown coating of copper deposits on the iron nails.
Equation: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) → FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)

practical_examples.title: Double Displacement (Barium Sulphate Precipitation)
practical_examples.problem: Write the reaction between sodium sulphate and barium chloride solutions.
practical_examples.solution:
When mixed, an exchange of ions occurs. A white precipitate of barium sulphate is formed along with sodium chloride in solution.
Equation: Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) → BaSO4(s)↓ + 2NaCl(aq)

practical_examples.title: Identifying Oxidation and Reduction
practical_examples.problem: In the reaction: CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O, identify the substance oxidized and the substance reduced.
practical_examples.solution:
Substance oxidized: H2 (It gains oxygen to become H2O).
Substance reduced: CuO (It loses oxygen to become Cu).
Oxidizing agent: CuO.
Reducing agent: H2.

practical_examples.title: Balancing Equation - Step by Step
practical_examples.problem: Balance the skeletal equation: HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 → Ca(NO3)2 + H2O
practical_examples.solution:
Step 1: Count atoms. LHS (H:3, N:1, O:5, Ca:1), RHS (H:2, N:2, O:7, Ca:1).
Step 2: Balance NO3 group. Put 2 before HNO3: 2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 → Ca(NO3)2 + H2O
Step 3: Now LHS has 4 H and 2 O (from OH). RHS has 2 H and 1 O (in H2O). Put 2 before H2O.
Step 4: Balanced Equation: 2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 → Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O

practical_examples.title: Balancing Equation - Complex
practical_examples.solution:
Step 1: Balance Fe by multiplying Fe by 3 (3Fe).
Step 2: Balance O by multiplying H2O by 4 (4H2O). Now we have 8 H atoms on LHS.
Step 3: Balance H by multiplying H2 by 4 (4H2).
Balanced: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) → Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g)

practical_examples.title: Prevention of Rancidity
practical_examples.problem: List methods to prevent rancidity in food items containing oils and fats.
practical_examples.solution:
1. Adding antioxidants (e.g., BHA, BHT).
2. Storing food in airtight containers.
3. Flushing bags of chips with nitrogen gas.
4. Keeping food in a refrigerator.

practical_examples.title: Exothermic vs Endothermic
practical_examples.problem: Classify the following as exothermic or endothermic: (a) Respiration (b) Photosynthesis
practical_examples.solution:
(a) Respiration is exothermic because glucose reacts with oxygen to release energy.
(b) Photosynthesis is endothermic because energy in the form of sunlight is absorbed by plants to create glucose.

previous_years_questions.question:
(a) Why is respiration considered an exothermic reaction?
(b) Define terms: (i) Rancidity (ii) Corrosion
previous_years_questions.solution:
(a) Respiration involves the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen, releasing a large amount of energy, hence it is exothermic.
(b) (i) Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils in food causing bad smell and taste. (ii) Corrosion is the slow degradation of metals due to attack by air, moisture, or acids.

previous_years_questions.question: Write the balanced chemical equation for the following reaction and identify the type of reaction: Potassium bromide (aq) + Barium iodide (aq) → Potassium iodide (aq) + Barium bromide (s)
previous_years_questions.solution:
Equation: 2KBr(aq) + BaI2(aq) → 2KI(aq) + BaBr2(s)
Type of reaction: Double displacement reaction (and Precipitation reaction, as BaBr2 can precipitate depending on conditions, though generally BaBr2 is soluble, the question implies a solid state).

previous_years_questions.question:
Identify the type of chemical reaction taking place in each of the following:
(i) Barium chloride solution is mixed with copper sulphate solution and a white precipitate is observed.
(ii) On heating copper powder in air in a china dish, the surface of copper powder turns black.
(iii) On heating green coloured ferrous sulphate crystals, reddish brown solid is left and smell of a gas having odour of burning sulphur is experienced.
(iv) Iron nails when left dipped in blue copper sulphate solution become brownish in colour and the blue colour of copper sulphate fades away.
(v) Quick lime reacts vigorously with water releasing a large amount of heat.
previous_years_questions.solution:
(i) Double displacement (Precipitation) reaction.
(ii) Oxidation (Combination) reaction.
(iii) Thermal decomposition reaction.
(iv) Displacement reaction.
(v) Combination (Exothermic) reaction.

previous_years_questions.question: Decomposition reactions require energy either in the form of heat or light or electricity for breaking down the reactants. Write one equation each for decomposition reactions where energy is supplied in the form of heat, light and electricity.
previous_years_questions.solution:
1. Heat: CaCO3(s) + Heat → CaO(s) + CO2(g)
2. Light: 2AgCl(s) + Sunlight → 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g)
3. Electricity: 2H2O(l) + Electricity → 2H2(g) + O2(g)

previous_years_questions.question: What is the colour of ferrous sulphate crystals? How does this colour change after heating?
previous_years_questions.solution: The initial colour of ferrous sulphate crystals (FeSO4.7H2O) is light green. Upon heating, it loses water of crystallisation and becomes dirty white/colourless, and further heating decomposes it into brown ferric oxide (Fe2O3).
